name: Foreskin restoration

card.summary: Foreskin restoration is the gradual stretching of remaining penile skin (or occasionally surgery) to recreate a covering over the glans after circumcision, which practitioners pursue for a natural-looking, covered appearance and for sensitivity and comfort.
card.note: Non-surgical restoration is described as poorly researched; the restored skin is a functional substitute, not an identical foreskin.

quick.overview:
Foreskin restoration recreates a covering of skin over the glans for men who were circumcised. Most people use non-surgical tissue expansion: remaining penile skin is held under gentle tension, by hand or with a device or tape, so that the body produces more skin over time. Surgical reconstruction using skin grafts also exists.

For appearance, the goal is a covered, uncircumcised look; people also cite sensitivity, comfort and protection of the glans. A 2023 survey of restorers cited by Wikipedia found increased glans sensitivity and sexual pleasure as common reasons, with 69% of respondents reporting more sexual pleasure. The method is described as poorly researched, and structures such as the frenulum and ridged band cannot be regrown.
quick.how: Practitioners describe a long, gradual routine of applying tension over months to years, using manual stretching, tape, cohesive bandage, weights or purpose-built restoration devices such as dual tension restorers or silicone air-inflation devices. Adjusting how tension is applied changes the ratio of outer to inner skin. Support groups such as NORM share experiences.
quick.risks: Care is needed not to injure or tear the skin while stretching. Surgical routes involve operative risks, and a 2023 surgical review cited by Wikipedia prefers tissue expansion partly because it avoids donor-site morbidity. Results vary with how much skin remains after circumcision, and the restored covering is a substitute rather than a reproduction of the original anatomy.

lead: Foreskin restoration is the process of recreating a foreskin lost to circumcision or injury, mainly through tissue expansion, with surgery as an alternative [1]. The most common approach is non-surgical: remaining penile skin is pulled forward over the glans and held under tension by hand or with a restoration device, which over time produces additional skin [1].

For appearance, restoration gives a covered glans in place of an exposed one, which participants describe as a more natural look. A 2023 survey of restorers named increased glans sensitivity, sexual pleasure and protection of the glans as common motivations, and 25% reported improved relationships [1]. Wikipedia describes restoration as producing a functional, though not identical, substitute for the prepuce; features such as the preputial orifice, ridged band and frenulum cannot be regrown [1].

The practice has ancient roots and a modern organised community. Greco-Roman culture prized intact genitals, and epispasm was used among some Jews in ancient Rome [1]. In 1989 the National Organization of Restoring Men (NORM) was founded, and UNCIRC, formed in 1991, merged into NORM in 1994 [1].

angle.text: Restoration works by tissue expansion, producing additional skin that covers the glans. People use it for a covered appearance and for the comfort and sensitivity they associate with having a covering.

paras: Non-surgical restoration relies on tissue expansion, which stimulates cell division, and regenerated tissue is said to share the attributes of the original [1]. Practitioners hold the skin forward by hand or with a device, and tension can be adjusted to change the ratio of outer to inner skin [1].

Surgical foreskin reconstruction usually grafts skin, often from the scrotum, onto the shaft; one described method is a four-stage procedure in which the shaft is buried in the scrotum for a period [1]. A 2023 surgical review cited by Wikipedia prefers tissue expansion because it avoids donor-site morbidity, noting that both expansion and grafting give acceptable appearance and long-term function [1]. Surgery can reduce the size of the opening after restoration, and longer expansion can help more skin gather at the tip [1].

In Greco-Roman culture, intact genitals were seen as beautiful, men with short foreskins sometimes wore a kynodesme, and epispasm aimed to lengthen the foreskin [1]. Under Antiochus Epiphanes (175-164 BCE), circumcision was outlawed and some Jews tried to undo theirs [1]. During the Bar Kokhba revolt (132-135 CE), rabbinic sources say those who restored were recircumcised [1]. During World War II some European Jews sought restoration to avoid persecution [1].

NORM was founded in 1989, UNCIRC in 1991 (merging into NORM in 1994), and NORM has chapters in the US, Canada, the UK, Australia, New Zealand and Germany; France has associations including AME and Droit au Corps [1]. The 2017 documentary American Circumcision covered restoration, and its subject estimated about 250,000 people worldwide were restoring in 2010 [1].

Motivations include dissatisfaction with circumcision and, for some intersex people with anatomical differences, a surgical option [1]. A 2023 survey reported that 69% of respondents experienced increased sexual pleasure and 25% improved relationships [1]. Support groups formed mainly in North America, where infant circumcision is routine [1]. The practice also appears in some looksmaxxing forum discussions, where members compare coverage and progress.

Wikipedia gives few details on risks beyond noting that care must be taken not to injure or tear the skin during expansion [1]. Surgical approaches add the risks of any grafting operation, including donor-site problems [1].

No studies found of controlled trials. Wikipedia states that non-surgical restoration, the most common method, remains poorly researched [1]. Evidence is limited to a 2023 survey of restorers and a 2023 surgical review comparing tissue expansion with grafting [1].
